title: Scotch Broth
subtitle: scottish lamb and barley soup
excerpt: Scotch broth is a thick, nourishing Scottish soup of lamb shoulder, root vegetables and pearl barley simmered together until the barley has thickened the broth. Serves 4 to 6.
sourceNotes: Scotch broth is one of Scotland's oldest dishes, documented in cookery books from the seventeenth century. It was peasant food that used every part of the animal and the cheapest vegetables available.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. The barley continues to absorb liquid; add extra water when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Makes a large pot naturally. Keeps in the fridge for up to 4 days and improves overnight.

glossaryTerms.definition: Hulled barley grains polished to a smooth pearl, which thicken soup as they cook.
A traditional Scottish soup of lamb and root vegetables thickened with barley.

content.text: is a meal in a bowl. Lamb shoulder gives the broth depth and collagen as it cooks slowly.
releases starch into the liquid as it softens, turning a thin stock into a thick, hearty soup that fills you up on a cold day.
The vegetables are added in stages so nothing turns to mush. Savoy cabbage goes in last, keeping some texture and its fresh flavour. Parsley stirred in at the end brightens the whole pot.
Put the lamb in the stockpot and cover with the water. Bring to a boil and skim off the grey foam that rises to the surface for the first few minutes.
Add the onion, carrot, celery, leek and rinsed pearl barley. Reduce to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook for 90 minutes.
Lift out the lamb and set aside to cool. When cool enough to handle, shred the meat from the bone. Discard any bone and excess fat.
Return the shredded lamb to the pot. Add the shredded savoy cabbage and simmer for 10 more minutes until tender.
Season well with black pepper. Stir in the chopped parsley and ladle into deep bowls. Serve with crusty bread.

attrs.problem: The broth is very thick and stodgy.
attrs.solution: The barley has absorbed a lot of liquid during cooking or storage. Add more water, stir well and re-season. The broth thickens as it stands.

attrs.problem: The lamb still has a gamey smell.
attrs.solution: Make sure you skimmed the foam properly at the start. The foam contains impurities and blood that cause an off flavour if left in.

attrs.problem: The vegetables are turning to mush.
attrs.solution: The simmer was too vigorous. Scotch broth needs a very gentle, slow simmer rather than a rolling boil.

content.text: Scotch broth is Scottish farmhouse food at its most fundamental. It is winter fuel, eaten with bread to make a full meal. Robert Burns wrote about it admiringly in the eighteenth century. It appears on Scottish pub menus as a starter but works best as a main course at home.
